claims.text: Hydride precursors must be decomposed at a controlled rate under ultra-high vacuum below 10^-6 Pa.
An inert atmosphere with oxygen gettering can substitute for ultra-high vacuum during hydride decomposition.
Maintaining oxygen partial pressure below 10^-8 Pa prevents brittle alpha-HCP and oxide formation.
Decomposition at 400-600 °C with a 1-5 °C/min ramp releases hydrogen slowly enough to avoid gas-evolution cracking.
Consolidation at 1200-1300 °C with a heating rate above 100 °C/min suppresses phase separation and grain growth.
Aging at 650-800 °C for 10-20 h can induce coherent nanoprecipitates.
The coherent precipitates strengthen the matrix through order hardening and dislocation pinning without initiating cracks.
Extrusion strain above 50% breaks up residual oxide clusters.
High-strain extrusion refines grains and produces Hall-Petch strengthening.
Rapid heating and cooling suppress HfO2 and HCP phases by preventing oxygen diffusion and segregation.
Low oxygen activity removes the thermodynamic driving force for alpha-HCP precipitation and oxide formation.
The proposed process will produce a fine-grained BCC matrix containing coherent nanoprecipitates while suppressing oxide and HCP phases.
The processed alloy will exceed 98% relative density.
The processed alloy will have oxygen content below 0.15 wt%.
The processed alloy will retain a single-phase BCC structure or a BCC matrix with coherent precipitates.
The proposed processing route will avoid catastrophic cracking.
The processed alloy will have a yield strength above 1.5 GPa at 800 °C.
The processed alloy will have room-temperature ductility above 10%.
The brittle-to-ductile transition temperature will be lower than in oxygen-contaminated samples.
Standard powder-metallurgy or uncontrolled hydride-sintering routes typically produce oxygen contents above 0.5 wt%.

contradictions.description: The prescribed hydride-decomposition stage uses a slow 1-5 °C/min ramp, whereas the experimental treatment is described broadly as ultra-high-vacuum processing with rapid heating at 100 °C/min. The design does not clearly restrict rapid heating to the later consolidation stage.

The predicted 800 °C yield strength is above 1.5 GPa, but the mechanism is declared falsified only if strength fails to exceed 1.0 GPa. Outcomes between 1.0 and 1.5 GPa would miss the prediction without satisfying the stated falsification rule.
